summary: Follow-up part for layer CA.4 (classical Diophantine equations). It plans what the first pass left open: the integral arithmetic of the Markoff level surfaces x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k after Ghosh–Sarnak (the group Γ, the Δ-function, admissible, exceptional and generic levels, class numbers, the descents, the fundamental sets of Theorem 1.1, the Cayley cubic, local solubility with corrected 2- and 3-adic lifts, the reciprocity obstruction, the families of Hasse failures and a certified enumeration), on one coefficient-one carrier shared with the Markoff–Hurwitz varieties Σx_i² = a∏x_i + k of Gamburd–Magee–Ronan (moves, exceptional families, the passage to positive tuples, Proposition 16 with corrected scope and the infinite descent) and with Chen's trace-coordinate surface (the twist ξ(y) = 3y, an isomorphism over ℤ[1/3], and Markoff's theorem in trace coordinates); the negative Pell radicands of Koymans–Pagano with rational solubility and Dirichlet's theorem for primes ≡ 1 (mod 4); and the Jacobi triple product with the cube, theta and Gauss identities in formal power series, as the formal counterpart of the analytic identity of GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic. It records four new mistakes in Ghosh–Sarnak and dispositions of the first pass's 45 review-frontier items.

nodes.title: Markoff–Hurwitz varieties V_{n,a,k} and their positive points
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, let R be a commutative ring and let a, k ∈ R. The Markoff–Hurwitz set is V_{n,a,k}(R) = {x : Fin n → R : x₁² + ⋯ + x_n² = a·x₁x₂⋯x_n + k}, the points over R of the affine hypersurface (1.1) of Gamburd–Magee–Ronan; tuples are ordered (indexed by Fin n) and no positivity is imposed. Over ℤ its positive part is V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊) = {x ∈ V_{n,a,k}(ℤ) : x_i > 0 for every i}. Two specialisations are the carriers of this layer: n = 3, a = 1 is the coefficient-one Markoff level surface x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k of Ghosh–Sarnak (CA.4/markoff-level-surface), and n = 3, a = 3, k = 0 is the coefficient-three Markoff surface X(R) of CA.4/markoff-triples.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; the results of Gamburd–Magee–Ronan take n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1 and k ∈ ℤ.
R is a commutative ring and a, k ∈ R; no field, characteristic or sign hypothesis.
The product is over all n coordinates; for n = 3 it is x₁x₂x₃.
proofSteps: Define V_{n,a,k}(R) as the zero set of F(x) = Σ_i x_i² − a·∏_i x_i − k on Fin n → R.
Functoriality: for a ring homomorphism f : R → S, F commutes with f coordinatewise, so f ∘ x lies in V_{n,f(a),f(k)}(S) for x ∈ V_{n,a,k}(R).
Symmetry: Σ x_i² and ∏ x_i are symmetric, so x ∘ σ ∈ V iff x ∈ V for every σ ∈ S_n; changing the signs of an even number of coordinates fixes both, so it preserves V.
Specialisations: for n = 3 the product over Fin 3 is x₁x₂x₃, so V_{3,1,k}(R) is the Markoff level set and V_{3,3,0}(R) is the coefficient-three set of CA.4/markoff-triples, by unfolding.
acceptance: Changing the sign of a single coordinate does not preserve V in general: (1, 1, 2) ∈ V_{3,3,0}(ℤ) but (−1, 1, 2) ∉ V_{3,3,0}(ℤ).

nodes.title: Markoff–Hurwitz moves and the group they generate with permutations and even sign changes
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, n ≥ 1 and a ∈ R. For j ∈ Fin n the move m_j : Rⁿ → Rⁿ replaces x_j by a·∏_{i≠j} x_i − x_j and fixes every other coordinate. Each m_j is an involution of Rⁿ and maps V_{n,a,k}(R) to itself for every k ∈ R, because x_j and a·∏_{i≠j}x_i − x_j are the two roots of T² − (a∏_{i≠j}x_i)·T + (Σ_{i≠j}x_i² − k). The Markoff–Hurwitz group Γ_{n,a}(R) is the subgroup of Equiv.Perm (Fin n → R) generated by the moves m_j, the coordinate permutations x ↦ x ∘ σ⁻¹ (σ ∈ S_n) and the even sign changes x ↦ (ε_i x_i)_i (ε_i = ±1, ∏ε_i = 1); its narrow subgroup is the subgroup generated by the permutations and even sign changes alone. Every element of Γ_{n,a}(R) maps V_{n,a,k}(R) to itself. For n = 3 and a = 1 the moves are Ghosh–Sarnak's Vieta involutions V_j and Γ_{3,1}(ℤ) is their group Γ; for n = 3 and a = 3 the moves are the coefficient-three moves R_j of CA.4/markoff-vieta-involution.
hypotheses: R commutative, a ∈ R; the moves are defined on all of Rⁿ.

Γ_{n,a}(R) is the group generated by the listed maps. The source's Aut(V) is the group of all polynomial automorphisms; that it equals the generated group (Horowitz for n = 3, Hu–Tan–Zhang for n ≥ 4) is not used: only the invariance of V(ℤ) under the generated group is.
proofSteps: Define m_j x = Function.update x j (a·∏_{i≠j} x_i − x_j); the product over i ≠ j does not involve x_j, so m_j(m_j x) = x and m_j is an involution (Function.Involutive.toPerm).
Preservation: Σ_i x_i² − a∏_i x_i is, as a polynomial in x_j, T² − (a∏_{i≠j}x_i)T + Σ_{i≠j}x_i²; the two roots have the same value, so m_j preserves every level set.
Permutations and even sign changes preserve V by the symmetry API of CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-variety; a subgroup generated by maps preserving a set preserves it (Subgroup.closure induction).
Specialisation: for n = 3 the product over i ≠ j is the product of the other two coordinates, giving V_j(x) = (x₂x₃ − x₁, x₂, x₃) and its cyclic analogues at a = 1, and R_j at a = 3.
Functoriality: a ring homomorphism f commutes with each generator, f ∘ m_j(x) = m_j(f ∘ x) (with parameter f(a)).
acceptance: For n = 3, a = 1: V₃(3, 3, 3) = (3, 3, 6), V₁(0, 1, 1) = (1, 1, 1) and V₂(1, 2, 3) = (1, 1, 3) (Ghosh–Sarnak's printed V₂ is corrected by ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E518).
The narrow subgroup of Γ_{3,a}(ℤ) acts on ℤ³ through a group of order 24 (S₃ and the four even sign patterns).

nodes.title: The Markoff level surfaces V_k and Chen's trace-coordinate surface X
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R and k ∈ R put M(x) = x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ and V_k(R) = {x ∈ R³ : M(x) = k}, the case n = 3, a = 1 of the Markoff–Hurwitz set (coordinates indexed by Fin 3 in the order x₁, x₂, x₃). The zero level X(R) := V_0(R) is the Markoff surface in trace coordinates of Chen, and X*(R) = X(R) ∖ {(0, 0, 0)}. Changing the sign of one coordinate identifies V_k(R) with the surface x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = k (Ghosh–Sarnak (9.6)); every permutation of the coordinates and every change of sign of two coordinates preserves V_k(R).
hypotheses: R commutative and k ∈ R; for the arithmetic results k ∈ ℤ and R = ℤ, ℤ_p or ℤ/p^nℤ.
The coefficient of x₁x₂x₃ is 1; the coefficient-three surface of CA.4/markoff-triples is a different scheme, related by the twist CA.4/markoff-coefficient-three-twist.
proofSteps: Define M as the polynomial above and V_k(R) as its fibre over k; by definition V_k(R) = V_{3,1,k}(R).
Symmetries: M is symmetric and M(−x₁, −x₂, x₃) = M(x); the substitution x₁ ↦ −x₁ turns M(x) = k into x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = k.
Functoriality is inherited from CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-variety.
acceptance: X(𝔽₃) = {(0, 0, 0)}, so X*(𝔽₃) is empty, whereas the coefficient-three surface has eight nonzero points over 𝔽₃.
|X*(𝔽_p)| = p(p + 3) for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and p(p − 3) for p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (from CA.4/markoff-type-point-count-mod-p with α = 1, β = 0).

nodes.title: The twist ξ(y) = 3y between the coefficient-three and coefficient-one Markoff surfaces
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R let X₃(R) = {y ∈ R³ : y₁² + y₂² + y₃² = 3y₁y₂y₃} be the coefficient-three set of CA.4/markoff-triples and X(R) = V₀(R). The map ξ(y) = 3y sends X₃(R) into X(R). It intertwines the moves: ξ(R_j y) = V_j(ξ y) for the coefficient-three moves R_j and the coefficient-one moves V_j, and it commutes with coordinate permutations and with every change of sign. If 3 is a unit in R, ξ is a bijection X₃(R) → X(R) with inverse x ↦ 3⁻¹x, so the two surfaces are isomorphic over ℤ[1/3]. Over ℤ, ξ is a bijection X₃(ℤ) → X(ℤ) (CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits). Over 𝔽₃, ξ is the zero map, X(𝔽₃) = {0} and X₃(𝔽₃) has nine points, so ξ is not an isomorphism of schemes over ℤ.
hypotheses: R is any commutative ring for the first two statements; 3 ∈ Rˣ for the inverse.
proofSteps: M(3y) = 9(y₁² + y₂² + y₃²) − 27y₁y₂y₃ = 9(y₁² + y₂² + y₃² − 3y₁y₂y₃), which vanishes on X₃(R).
Moves: V_j(3y)_j = 9y_{j+1}y_{j+2} − 3y_j = 3(3y_{j+1}y_{j+2} − y_j) = 3·(R_j y)_j, and the other coordinates agree.
If 3 is a unit, the same computation run backwards shows that 3⁻¹x ∈ X₃(R) for x ∈ X(R), and the two maps are inverse.

Over 𝔽₃: M(x) = x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = 0 forces x = 0 (if all coordinates are nonzero the squares sum to 0 but the product is ±1; if one vanishes the other two squares sum to 0, so both vanish), while X₃(𝔽₃) = {0} ∪ {±1}³.
acceptance: Over ℤ[1/3] the inverse sends (3, 3, 3) to (1, 1, 1).

nodes.title: Markoff's theorem in trace coordinates: the positive points of X form one orbit
nodes.statement: The positive integral points of X: x² + y² + z² = xyz (all three coordinates > 0) are exactly the points obtained from (3, 3, 3) by finite words in the coefficient-one moves V₁, V₂, V₃; in particular they form a single orbit of the group generated by the moves and the coordinate permutations (Chen's Γ), and every move maps a positive point to a positive point. Together with CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits, X(ℤ) is the union of the two Γ_{3,1}(ℤ)-orbits {0} and Γ_{3,1}(ℤ)·(3, 3, 3).
hypotheses: Integral points; positivity of all three coordinates.
Chen's Γ (moves and permutations) has no sign changes; the sign changes are needed only for the statement about all of X(ℤ).
proofSteps: ξ of CA.4/markoff-coefficient-three-twist maps the positive Markoff triples M of CA.4/positive-markoff-triples bijectively onto the positive points of X(ℤ): it maps positive to positive, and conversely every coordinate of an integral point of X is divisible by 3 (CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits).
By CA.4/markoff-root-generation every y ∈ M is a word R_{i₁}⋯R_{i_k}(1, 1, 1); applying ξ and the intertwining ξ ∘ R_j = V_j ∘ ξ gives ξ(y) = V_{i₁}⋯V_{i_k}(3, 3, 3).
Moves preserve positivity: if x ∈ X(ℤ) is positive then V_j(x)_j = (x_{j+1}² + x_{j+2}²)/x_j > 0, the other root of the quadratic.
For all of X(ℤ): a nonzero integral point has no zero coordinate and an even number of negative coordinates (its coordinate product is a sum of squares), so a double sign change makes it positive.
acceptance: Up to order, the positive points of X with largest coordinate at most 100 are (3, 3, 3), (3, 3, 6), (3, 6, 15), (3, 15, 39) and (6, 15, 87), the images under ξ of the Markoff triples with largest entry at most 33.

nodes.title: Ghosh–Sarnak's Δ-function from Bhargava cubes
nodes.statement: For x = (x₁, x₂, x₃) in a commutative ring put Δ(x) = (1 + x₂² − x₁² − x₃²)² − 4(x₁x₃ − x₂)². Then Δ(x) = (1 + x₁ + x₂ + x₃)(1 + x₂ − x₁ − x₃)(1 + x₃ − x₁ − x₂)(1 + x₁ − x₂ − x₃), and Δ is the common discriminant B² − 4AC of the three binary quadratic forms Q_i(u, v) = (x_jx_l − x_i)u² + (1 + x_i² − x_j² − x_l²)uv + (x_jx_l − x_i)v² ({i, j, l} = {1, 2, 3}) obtained from the three slicings of the Bhargava cube with entries 1, x₁, x₂, x₃. Δ is invariant under coordinate permutations and under changing the signs of two coordinates. Over ℤ: Δ(x) ≡ 0 (mod 4) if x₁² + x₂² + x₃² is odd and Δ(x) ≡ 1 (mod 4) if it is even; and if 2 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ then Δ(x) < 0 if and only if x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁ + x₂ − 2.
hypotheses: Polynomial identities over any commutative ring; the congruence and sign statements over ℤ.
Only the polynomial Δ is used in the rest of the layer; the Bhargava cube is the source's motivation and enters only through the discriminant identity.
proofSteps: Expand both sides of the factorisation (a polynomial identity in ℤ[x₁, x₂, x₃]); equivalently, the first form is a difference of squares (P − 2Q)(P + 2Q) with P = 1 + x₂² − x₁² − x₃² and Q = x₁x₃ − x₂, and each factor splits further.
Discriminants: for Q_i the discriminant (1 + x_i² − x_j² − x_l²)² − 4(x_jx_l − x_i)² equals Δ by the symmetry of the factorised form.
Invariance: the factorised form is permuted by S₃ and by (x₁, x₂, x₃) ↦ (−x₁, −x₂, x₃) (which swaps the pairs of factors).
Mod 4: with s = x₁² + x₂² + x₃², P ≡ 1 + s (mod 2) and 4Q² ≡ 0 (mod 4), so Δ ≡ P² (mod 4) is 0 if s is odd and 1 if s is even.

Sign: for 2 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ the factor 1 + x₁ + x₂ + x₃ is positive while 1 + x₂ − x₁ − x₃ ≤ −1 and 1 + x₁ − x₂ − x₃ ≤ 1 − x₁ < 0; so Δ has the sign of 1 + x₃ − x₁ − x₂, which is negative iff x₃ ≤ x₁ + x₂ − 2 (and Δ = 0 iff x₃ = x₁ + x₂ − 1). The criterion was also checked for 2 ≤ x₁ ≤ 40, x₂ ≤ 60, x₃ ≤ 120 by computation.
acceptance: Δ(3, 3, 6) = 325: Δ is not invariant under the Vieta moves (Δ(3, 3, 3) = −80); its change under them is CA.4/markoff-delta-differences.

nodes.title: The Δ-differences of the Vieta moves on a level surface
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, k ∈ R and x ∈ V_k(R), and let {i, j, l} = {1, 2, 3}. Then (1) (x_j² − 4)(x_l² − 4) = (2x_i − x_jx_l)² − 4(k − 4), and (2) Δ(V_i x) − Δ(x) = x_jx_l(x_jx_l − 2x_i)·[2(k − 5) + (x_j² − 4)(x_l² − 4)]. Over ℤ the bracket in (2) is strictly positive in each of two cases: k < 0 (for every x ∈ V_k(ℤ)), and k ≥ 5 with |x_j|, |x_l| ≥ 3. Hence, for such x, the sign of Δ(V_i x) − Δ(x) is the sign of x_jx_l(x_jx_l − 2x_i).
hypotheses: x ∈ V_k(R); the identities are polynomial identities modulo M(x) − k.
For the positivity statements R = ℤ and k is an integer.
proofSteps: (1): expand (2x_i − x_jx_l)² = 4x_i² − 4x_ix_jx_l + x_j²x_l² and replace 4x_i² − 4x_ix_jx_l by 4(k − x_j² − x_l²) using M(x) = k.

(2): V_i changes only x_i, to x_jx_l − x_i; write Δ in the factorised form of CA.4/markoff-delta and reduce Δ(V_i x) − Δ(x) modulo M(x) − k (a polynomial computation, checked on 20000 random integral points of their own level sets).
k < 0: by (1) the bracket is (2x_i − x_jx_l)² − 2k + 6 > 0.
k ≥ 5 and |x_j|, |x_l| ≥ 3: then (x_j² − 4)(x_l² − 4) ≥ 25 and 2(k − 5) ≥ 0.

Identity (1) is equation (8.2) of the source (with d = k − 4), used for the reciprocity obstructions.

nodes.title: The Δ-minimum on the zero level: Δ < 0 exactly at the narrow class of (3, 3, 3)
nodes.statement: For x ∈ V₀(ℤ): Δ(x) < 0 if and only if x is narrowly equivalent to (3, 3, 3) (a permutation of it with two signs changed), and then Δ(x) = −80; Δ(0, 0, 0) = 1; and Δ(x) ≥ 0 at every other point. Consequently, on each of the two Γ-orbits of V₀(ℤ) (CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits) the function Δ attains its minimum exactly on one narrow-equivalence class, the class of the orbit's root (0, 0, 0) or (3, 3, 3).
hypotheses: Integral points of the zero level; narrow equivalence is the action of permutations and double sign changes.
proofSteps: A nonzero x ∈ V₀(ℤ) has an even number of negative coordinates, so it is narrowly equivalent to a positive point; Δ is a narrow invariant (CA.4/markoff-delta), so assume 1 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃.
Then (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) − 16 = (2x₃ − x₁x₂)² (identity (1) of CA.4/markoff-delta-differences at k = 0) forces x₁ ≥ 3.

If Δ(x) < 0 then x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁ + x₂ − 2 < 2x₂ (sign criterion of CA.4/markoff-delta). Solving 2x₃ = x₁x₂ ± σ with σ² = x₁²x₂² − 4(x₁² + x₂²): for x₁ ≥ 4 the + sign contradicts x₃ < 2x₂, and the − sign gives 4x₂² ≤ x₁x₂² ≤ x₁² + 2x₂² ≤ 3x₂², a contradiction.
For x₁ = 3 the bound gives x₃ ∈ {x₂, x₂ + 1}; x₃ = x₂ forces x₂ = 3, and x₃ = x₂ + 1 gives 9 + x₂² + (x₂ + 1)² = 3x₂(x₂ + 1), which has no integral solution.
acceptance: The two orbits have minima Δ = 1 (at 0) and Δ = −80 (at the narrow class of (3, 3, 3)).

sources.match: On the zero level Δ is negative only at (3, 3, 3) up to narrow equivalence, Δ(0, 0, 0) = 1 and Δ(3, 3, 3) = −80, so each of Markoff's two orbits has a unique Δ-minimising root.

nodes.title: Admissible, exceptional and generic levels, and Hasse failures
nodes.statement: For k ∈ ℤ: k is admissible if k ≢ 3 (mod 4) and k ≢ ±3 (mod 9); k is exceptional if some x ∈ V_k(ℤ) has a coordinate in {0, ±1, ±2}; k is generic if it is admissible and not exceptional; and k is a Hasse failure if it is admissible and V_k(ℤ) = ∅. Equivalently, k is exceptional if and only if k = u² + v², or 4(k − 1) = u² + 3v², or k − 4 = u², for some u, v ∈ ℤ (the three cases being a coordinate 0, ±1 and ±2). Every admissible k < 0 is generic, and an exceptional k is never a Hasse failure.
hypotheses: Integers k; exceptionality refers to integral points only.

This exceptional notion (a point with a small coordinate) is Ghosh–Sarnak's; it is different from Gamburd–Magee–Ronan's exceptional families (CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-exceptional), which for n = 3, a = 1 are only the coordinate-±2 case.
proofSteps: Define the four predicates as stated; admissibility is decidable from k mod 36.

Characterisation: x₁ = 0 gives x₂² + x₃² = k; x₁ = ±1 gives x₂² ∓ x₂x₃ + x₃² = k − 1, i.e. (2x₂ ∓ x₃)² + 3x₃² = 4(k − 1); x₁ = ±2 gives (x₂ ∓ x₃)² = k − 4; conversely each solution gives a point, using the permutation symmetry for the other coordinates.
For k < 0 none of the three equations is solvable (the left sides are ≥ 0 while k < 0, 4(k − 1) < 0 and k − 4 < 0), so no point has a small coordinate.
An exceptional k has an integral point, so it is not a Hasse failure.
acceptance: 46 is generic: it is admissible, not a sum of two squares, 4·45 = 180 is not of the form u² + 3v², and 42 is not a square.
5 is exceptional ((0, 1, 2) ∈ V₅(ℤ)); 3 and 6 are not admissible; −4 is generic and a Hasse failure.

nodes.title: Markoff class numbers h_M(k) and the fundamental sets F^±_k
nodes.statement: Let Γ = Γ_{3,1}(ℤ) act on ℤ³ (CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-moves). For k ∈ ℤ the orbit set of V_k(ℤ) is the set of Γ-orbits meeting V_k(ℤ) (each such orbit lies in V_k(ℤ)); h_M(k) is its cardinality, finite for k ≠ 4 (CA.4/markoff-class-number-finite) and zero exactly when V_k(ℤ) = ∅. The fundamental sets are F⁺_k(ℤ) = {u ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ u₃, u₁² + u₂² + u₃² + u₁u₂u₃ = k} and F⁻_k(ℤ) = {u ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ u₃ ≤ u₁u₂/2, u₁² + u₂² + u₃² − u₁u₂u₃ = k}, with h⁺(k) = |F⁺_k(ℤ)| and h⁻(k) = |F⁻_k(ℤ)|; both sets are finite. Two points are narrowly equivalent if one is obtained from the other by a permutation and a change of sign of two coordinates. The points (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ) form the set S⁺(k) of the descent, and S⁻(k) = F⁻_k(ℤ).
hypotheses: k ∈ ℤ; the class number is a natural number by the convention Nat.card, so for k = 4 (infinitely many orbits) statements use the orbit set itself, not h_M(4).
F⁺_k is relevant for k ≥ 5 and F⁻_k for k < 0; F⁺_k(ℤ) = ∅ for k < 54, since u₁² + u₂² + u₃² + u₁u₂u₃ ≥ 54 when every u_j ≥ 3.
proofSteps: Define the orbit set as the image of V_k(ℤ) in MulAction.orbitRel.Quotient Γ (Fin 3 → ℤ), and h_M(k) as its Nat.card.
Each orbit meeting V_k(ℤ) lies in V_k(ℤ), because Γ preserves V_k(ℤ) (CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-moves).

Finiteness of F⁺_k: 3u₁² + u₁³ ≤ k bounds u₁, then u₁² + 2u₂² + u₁u₂² ≤ k bounds u₂, and u₃ is a root of a quadratic. Finiteness of F⁻_k: u₃ ≤ u₁u₂/2 makes u₃ the smaller root of u₃² − u₁u₂u₃ + u₁² + u₂² − k, and u₃ ≥ u₂ then gives (u₁ − 2)u₂² ≤ u₁² − k, which bounds u₂ (and u₁ ≤ u₂) in terms of |k|; this is the box of CA.4/markoff-descent-negative-level.
h_M(k) = 0 iff V_k(ℤ) = ∅, since the orbit set is empty exactly then.
acceptance: h_M(0) = 2 (CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits); F⁺₅₄(ℤ) = {(3, 3, 3)}; |F⁺₃₆₈₅(ℤ)| = 6 and |F⁻₋₃₆₉₁(ℤ)| = 9 (the examples of Ghosh–Sarnak's Figures 1–4, recomputed); 3685 is exceptional ((1, 32, 70) ∈ V₃₆₈₅(ℤ)), so h_M(3685) ≥ 7 (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E554).
F⁺₅(ℤ) = ∅ while (0, 1, 2) ∈ V₅(ℤ), so h⁺ and h_M differ at exceptional levels.

nodes.title: Descent on V_k(ℤ) for k ≥ 5 (Ghosh–Sarnak, Lemma 2.1)
nodes.statement: (a) Let k ≥ 1 be an integer. If 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ and x ∈ V_k(ℤ), then x₁x₂ − x₃ < x₂. (b) Let k ≥ 5. Every point of V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent either to a point having a coordinate in {0, ±1, ±2} or to a point (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ). In particular, for k ≥ 5 not exceptional, every point of V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a point of S⁺(k).
hypotheses: k ≥ 1 for (a) (the source's estimate needs only k > 0 and x₁ ≥ 3); k ≥ 5 for (b) (the source states k > 4).
The descent applies the move V₃ to a narrowly reduced positive point; small-coordinate points are kept as a separate branch (including coordinate ±2), not assumed to lie in S⁺(k).
proofSteps: Narrow reduction: a point with no zero coordinate is narrowly equivalent to one with all coordinates positive or with exactly one negative coordinate; sort the absolute values.

(a) The roots of c² − x₁x₂c + x₁² + x₂² − k are x₃ and x₁x₂ − x₃, namely (x₁x₂ ± σ)/2 with σ² = x₁²x₂² − 4(x₁² + x₂² − k). If x₁x₂ − x₃ ≥ x₂, the smaller root is ≥ x₂ (it is x₃ if 2x₃ ≤ x₁x₂, and x₁x₂ − x₃ otherwise), so σ ≤ (x₁ − 2)x₂; squaring gives (x₁ − 2)x₂² ≤ x₁² − k < x₁² ≤ x₂², impossible for x₁ ≥ 3. Only k ≥ 1 is used, so (a) holds for every k ≥ 1.

(b) For a sorted positive point with x₁ ≥ 3 apply V₃: the new third coordinate x₁x₂ − x₃ is negative (giving a one-negative point, which is in S⁺(k) after sorting if all absolute values are ≥ 3), or in {0, 1, 2} (a small coordinate), or ≥ 3 and < x₂ by (a), giving a positive point whose coordinate sum is smaller (x₁x₂ − x₃ < x₂ ≤ x₃).

The coordinate sum (Hurwitz's height x₁ + x₂ + x₃) strictly decreases along the positive branch, so the process stops; a one-negative point with all absolute values ≥ 3 is (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ) after a narrow move.
acceptance: k = 9454 (generic): every integral point descends to one of the eleven points of S⁺(9454).
k = 5: the descent ends at the small-coordinate point (0, 1, 2), and S⁺(5) is empty.

nodes.title: The levels k = 1, 2, 3: one finite orbit, one finite orbit, no points
nodes.statement: V₃(ℤ) = ∅. V₂(ℤ) is a single Γ-orbit, that of (0, 1, 1); it is finite, with 16 points: the twelve points with one coordinate 0 and the other two ±1, and the four points (±1, ±1, ±1) with an even number of minus signs. V₁(ℤ) is a single Γ-orbit, that of (0, 0, 1), consisting of the six points ±e_i. Hence h_M(1) = h_M(2) = 1 and h_M(3) = 0.
hypotheses: Integral points; Γ = Γ_{3,1}(ℤ).
proofSteps: k = 3: M(x) ≡ 3 (mod 4) has no solution (squares are 0, 1 mod 4; a case check over (ℤ/4ℤ)³).

For 1 ≤ k ≤ 4, a one-negative point (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u_j ≥ 1 has u₁² + u₂² + u₃² + u₁u₂u₃ ≥ 4, which leaves only (−1, 1, 1) at k = 4; so for k ≤ 3 every point without a zero coordinate is narrowly positive, and the descent estimate of CA.4/markoff-descent-positive-level (valid for every k > 0 when x₁ ≥ 3) reduces it to a point with a coordinate ≤ 2.

Small coordinates: for k = 1 they give ±e_i only; for k = 2 they give the 16 listed points; these sets are closed under V₁, V₂, V₃, permutations and double sign changes (direct computation: V₁(0, 1, 1) = (1, 1, 1), V₁(1, 1, 1) = (0, 1, 1)), so each is one orbit and V_k(ℤ) has no other point.
acceptance: Γ·(0, 1, 1) has exactly 16 points; this corrects the source's statement that this orbit is infinite (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E551).
All integral points of V₂ with |x_i| ≤ 40 are the 16 listed ones (computation).

nodes.title: Descent on V_k(ℤ) for k < 0 (Ghosh–Sarnak, Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let k < 0. No point of V_k(ℤ) has a coordinate in {0, ±1, ±2}; every point of V_k(ℤ) is narrowly equivalent to a point with 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃; and every point of V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a point of S⁻(k) = F⁻_k(ℤ). Moreover F⁻_k(ℤ) lies in the box U(k) = {3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ √(|k| + 9), 3 ≤ x₃ ≤ (|k| + 9)/2}, so it is finite (the source states the weaker bound x₃ ≤ (3/2)(|k| + 9)).
hypotheses: k < 0, integral points.
proofSteps: Small coordinates: x₁ = 0, ±1, ±2 would give x₂² + x₃² = k, (2x₂ ∓ x₃)² + 3x₃² = 4(k − 1) or (x₂ ∓ x₃)² = k − 4, all impossible for k < 0.
Signs: M(x) = k < 0 forces x₁x₂x₃ > x₁² + x₂² + x₃² > 0, so an even number of coordinates is negative and a double sign change makes all positive.

Descent: for a sorted positive point with x₃ > x₁x₂/2, the move V₃ gives x₁x₂ − x₃ < x₃; it is ≥ 3 (no small coordinates, and it is positive since otherwise M would be ≥ 0), so the point (x₁, x₂, x₁x₂ − x₃) has smaller coordinate sum; after sorting, iterate until x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2.

Box: if x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2 then (x₁ − 2)x₂² ≤ x₁² − k; for x₁ ≥ 4 this gives x₂² ≤ |k|, and for x₁ = 3 the smaller root of x₃² − 3x₂x₃ + x₂² + 9 − k must be ≥ x₂, which gives x₂² ≤ 9 + |k|; finally x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2 ≤ x₂²/2.
acceptance: For −3691 ≤ k ≤ −1 every point of F⁻_k(ℤ) lies in U(k) (computation).

sources.locator: §2, Lemma 2.2 and the preceding paragraph, p. 10
sources.match: For k < 0 there are no coordinates 0, 1, 2; every point is equivalent to one of the compact set S⁻(k) inside the box U(k), by the same estimate (x₁ − 2)x₂² ≤ x₁² − k and the descent x₃ ↦ x₁x₂ − x₃.

nodes.title: Ghosh–Sarnak's theorem on fundamental sets (Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: (i) Let k ≥ 5 be an integer that is not exceptional. The map u ↦ Γ·(−u₁, u₂, u₃) is a bijection from F⁺_k(ℤ) onto the set of Γ-orbits of V_k(ℤ): the points (−u₁, u₂, u₃), u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ), are pairwise Γ-inequivalent and every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to exactly one of them. (ii) Let k < 0. The map u ↦ Γ·u is a bijection from F⁻_k(ℤ) onto the set of Γ-orbits of V_k(ℤ). Hence h_M(k) = h⁺(k) in case (i) and h_M(k) = h⁻(k) in case (ii); in particular h_M(k) is finite and is computed by a finite search.
hypotheses: (i) k ≥ 5 not exceptional (the source assumes k generic; for k not admissible both sides are empty).
(ii) every k < 0 (the source assumes k admissible; otherwise both sides are empty).
At exceptional levels k ≥ 5 the map in (i) is still injective (CA.4/markoff-positive-root-orbits) but not onto (CA.4/markoff-exceptional-class-number-lower-bound).
proofSteps: Surjectivity in (i): by CA.4/markoff-descent-positive-level, since k is not exceptional no point has a small coordinate, so every point is equivalent to a point of S⁺(k).

Injectivity in (i): CA.4/markoff-positive-root-orbits (the Δ-ordering: a negative node has three Δ-larger neighbours, a positive node exactly one Δ-smaller neighbour, so each component of the Vieta graph modulo narrow equivalence has one negative root).
Surjectivity in (ii): CA.4/markoff-descent-negative-level.

Injectivity in (ii): by CA.4/markoff-delta-differences all brackets are positive for k < 0, so the sign of Δ(V_i x) − Δ(x) is that of x_jx_l − 2x_i; at a sorted point the first two are positive and the third is ≥ 0 exactly on S⁻(k). So the points of S⁻(k) are the Δ-minimal nodes and every other node has exactly one Δ-smaller neighbour; a path between two distinct points of S⁻(k) in the Vieta tree would have a vertex of maximal Δ with two smaller neighbours.
acceptance: h_M(9454) = 11 and h_M(9500) = 8 (generic levels from the source's Table 5) and h_M(−3691) = 9 (the source's illustration, recomputed); the source's other illustration, k = 3685, is exceptional, where (i) does not apply (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E554).
h_M(46) = 0 since 46 is generic and F⁺₄₆(ℤ) = ∅; h_M(−2) = 1 with representative (3, 3, 4).

sources.match: For generic k ≥ 5 every integral point is Γ-equivalent to a unique (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u in F⁺_k, and for admissible k < 0 to a unique point of F⁻_k; the points of each fundamental set are inequivalent.
The proof: the descent lemmas give existence, and the signs of the Δ-differences show that each component of the Vieta tree has a unique Δ-minimal root.

nodes.title: Finitely many orbits on every level except the Cayley cubic
nodes.statement: For every integer k ≠ 4, V_k(ℤ) is the union of finitely many Γ-orbits, so h_M(k) is the number of orbits. For k = 4 there are infinitely many orbits (CA.4/markoff-cayley-cubic-orbits).
hypotheses: k ∈ ℤ, k ≠ 4; includes exceptional levels k ≥ 5 and the levels 0 ≤ k ≤ 3.
proofSteps: k < 0: CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets (ii) and finiteness of F⁻_k(ℤ).
k = 0: two orbits (CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits); 1 ≤ k ≤ 3: CA.4/markoff-levels-one-to-three.

k ≥ 5: by CA.4/markoff-descent-positive-level every orbit meets the finite set S⁺(k) or the small-coordinate locus. Points with a coordinate 0 or ±1 are finite in number (positive definite binary forms x₂² + x₃² = k and x₂² ∓ x₂x₃ + x₃² = k − 1). Points with a coordinate ±2 exist only if k − 4 = w² is a square, w > 0, and are, up to narrow equivalence, (2, t, t + w), t ∈ ℤ; the move V₂ followed by a transposition sends (2, t, t + w) to (2, t + w, t + 2w), so these points fall into at most w orbits.
A finite set meets only finitely many orbits.
acceptance: h_M(5) is finite although 5 − 4 = 1 is a square: the points (2, t, t + 1) lie in one orbit.
k = 13 = 4 + 3²: the line (2, t, t + 3) meets at most three orbits (a computation finds two).

nodes.title: The Cayley cubic k = 4: one orbit for each (2, a, a)
nodes.statement: Every Γ-orbit of V₄(ℤ) contains exactly one narrow-equivalence class of the form (2, a, a) with a ≥ 0, so V₄(ℤ) has infinitely many orbits. The orbit of (2, 0, 0) is its narrow class (it contains (−2, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 2)); the orbit of (2, 1, 1) consists of the two narrow classes of (2, 1, 1) and (−1, 1, 1). On every orbit Δ attains its minimum at a unique narrow class: Δ(−2, 0, 0) = 9, Δ(−1, 1, 1) = −16 and Δ(2, a, a) = 9 − 4a² for a ≥ 2.
hypotheses: k = 4, integral points; the points (2, a, a) are fixed by V₂ and V₃.
proofSteps: One-negative points (−x₁, x₂, x₃) with x_j ≥ 0 and x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = 4 are, up to narrow equivalence, (−2, 0, 0) and (−1, 1, 1).

Positive sorted points with x₁ = 0 or 1 are (0, 0, 2) and (1, 1, 2); for x₁ ≥ 3 the descent of CA.4/markoff-descent-positive-level (its inequality holds for k = 4 when x₁ ≥ 3) reaches a point with a coordinate 2, and a point with a coordinate 2 has the form (2, a, a) since (x₂ − x₃)² = k − 4 = 0.

Inequivalence: by CA.4/markoff-delta-differences at k = 4, two moves fix (2, a, a) and the third goes up in Δ to a point not of the same form, while at a point with all coordinates ≥ 3 two moves go up and one goes down; so a component of the Vieta graph contains at most one class (2, a, a). The orbits of (2, 0, 0), (2, 1, 1), (2, 2, 2) are checked directly.
Δ-minimum: Δ(2, a, a) = 9 − 4a² < 0 for a ≥ 2 and, as at k = 0, Δ ≥ 0 at every other point of its orbit.
acceptance: The orbit of (2, 1, 1) is the two narrow classes of (2, 1, 1) and (1, 1, −1) (computation).

nodes.title: Explicit points on V_k over rings in which 2 and 3 are units (Ghosh–Sarnak, Corollary 6.3)
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring in which 2 and 3 are units and let k ∈ R. Put e = 2, f = e⁻¹ = 1/2, c = (e − f)⁻² = 4/9 and x₁ = 2 − (k − 4)c, x₂ = e + f, x₃ = e − f + f·x₁. Then M(x₁, x₂, x₃) = k, so V_k(R) ≠ ∅. In particular M(x) ≡ k (mod pⁿ) is soluble for every prime p ≥ 5, every n ≥ 1 and every integer k, and V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for p ≥ 5.
hypotheses: 2, 3 ∈ Rˣ (for R = ℤ/pⁿℤ this is p ≥ 5); e − f = 3/2 is then a unit.
proofSteps: Direct algebra: substitute x₁ = 2 − (k − 4)c, x₂ = e + f, x₃ = e − f + f x₁ into M with ef = 1 and c(e − f)² = 1; the expression reduces to k (the source obtains the same point from the trace identity tr(A)² + tr(B)² + tr(AB)² − tr(A)tr(B)tr(AB) = tr[A, B] + 2 with B = diag(e, f) and A = [[1, 2 − t], [c, 1 + (2 − t)c]]; the trace identity itself is not needed).
For R = ℤ/pⁿℤ with p ≥ 5, and for R = ℤ_p with p ≥ 5, 2 and 3 are units.
acceptance: Checked for p ∈ {5, 7, 11, 13}, n ∈ {1, 2} and 0 ≤ k < 40 (computation).
Over ℤ_p with p ≥ 5 the formula gives an exact p-adic point for every k ∈ ℤ_p, so no Hensel lifting is needed at these primes.

nodes.title: The quadratic exponential sum S_p(a) and its comparison with Mathlib's Gauss sums
nodes.statement: For an odd prime p let ψ = ZMod.stdAddChar : ℤ/pℤ → ℂ (ψ(t) = e^{2πit/p}), χ the quadratic character of 𝔽_p with values in ℂ, and S_p(a) = Σ_{u ∈ 𝔽_p} ψ(a u²). Then (i) S_p(0) = p; (ii) S_p(a) = χ(a)·S_p(1) for a ≠ 0; (iii) S_p(1) = gaussSum χ ψ; (iv) S_p(1)² = χ(−1)·p; (v) Σ_{a ∈ 𝔽_p} χ(a)ψ(ab) = χ(b)·S_p(1) for every b; (vi) Σ_{x ∈ 𝔽_p} χ(c − x²) = −χ(−1) for every c ≠ 0.
hypotheses: p an odd prime; ψ is the standard primitive additive character; χ is quadraticChar (ZMod p) composed with ℤ → ℂ.
proofSteps: (i) is immediate. For (ii)–(iii): Σ_u ψ(au²) = Σ_t (1 + χ(t))ψ(at) by quadraticChar_card_sqrts; Σ_t ψ(at) = 0 for a ≠ 0 (AddChar.sum_mulShift), and Σ_t χ(t)ψ(at) = χ(a)⁻¹·gaussSum χ ψ = χ(a)·gaussSum χ ψ (gaussSum_mulShift, χ(a)² = 1).
(iv) is gaussSum_sq for the nontrivial quadratic character χ and the primitive character ψ.
(v) is the same computation as (iii) with the roles of the variables exchanged, using χ(0) = 0 for b = 0.

(vi): Σ_x χ(c − x²) = Σ_y χ(y)·#{x : x² = c − y} = Σ_y χ(y)(1 + χ(c − y)) = Σ_y χ(y(c − y)), since Σ_y χ(y) = 0 (quadraticChar_sum_zero). For y ≠ 0, χ(y(c − y)) = χ(y²)χ(c/y − 1) = χ(c/y − 1), and y ↦ c/y − 1 is a bijection from 𝔽_p^× onto 𝔽_p ∖ {−1}; so the sum is Σ_t χ(t) − χ(−1) = −χ(−1).
acceptance: S₅(1) = √5 and S₅(2) = −√5 (2 is a non-residue modulo 5).

nodes.title: Points of x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − αx₁x₂x₃ = β over 𝔽_p (Ghosh–Sarnak, Lemma 6.4)
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime, α, β ∈ 𝔽_p and N_p = #{x ∈ 𝔽_p³ : x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − αx₁x₂x₃ = β}. Then N_p = p² + p·χ(−β) if α = 0, and N_p = p² + 1 + p·χ(α²β − 4)·(3 + χ(β)) if α ≠ 0, where χ is the quadratic character (χ(0) = 0). Consequently N_p ≥ (p − 2)² − 3 > 0 for p ≥ 5, N₃ > 0 for all α, β, and |X*(𝔽_p)| = p² + 3p·χ(−1), that is p(p + 3) for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and p(p − 3) for p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
hypotheses: p odd prime; α, β ∈ 𝔽_p arbitrary.
proofSteps: Reduction: for α ≠ 0 the substitution y = αx turns the equation into y₁² + y₂² + y₃² − y₁y₂y₃ = α²β, so it suffices to treat α ∈ {0, 1}.

α = 1: with u = 2x₃ − x₁x₂ the count equals that of 4(x₁² + x₂²) + u² − x₁²x₂² = 4β; detect the equation by orthogonality of ψ and expand with S_p (CA.4/quadratic-gauss-sum-normalisation), giving N_p − p² = (1/p)Σ_{a≠0} T_p(a)S_p(a)ψ(−4aβ) with T_p(a) = Σ_{x₁} ψ(4ax₁²)S_p(a(4 − x₁²)).

Split x₁ = ±2 from the other values, use S_p(a(4 − x₁²)) = χ(a(4 − x₁²))S_p(1), sum over a with (v) of the normalisation node and evaluate Σ_x χ(4 − x²) = −χ(−1) by (vi); with S_p(1)² = χ(−1)p this gives p² + 1 + p·χ(β − 4)(3 + χ(β)).
α = 0: N_p − p² = (1/p)Σ_{a≠0}ψ(−βa)S_p(a)³ = (S_p(1)³/p)Σ_a χ(a)ψ(−βa) = p·χ(−β).
Lower bound: |χ(·)| ≤ 1 gives N_p ≥ p² − 4p + 1 when α ≠ 0 and N_p ≥ p² − p when α = 0; for p = 3 check the nine pairs (α, β).
acceptance: Checked against direct enumeration for all α, β and p ∈ {3, 5, 7, 11, 13} (computation).

nodes.title: Local solubility of the Markoff equation (Ghosh–Sarnak, Proposition 6.1)
nodes.statement: Let k ∈ ℤ. (a) For a prime p ≥ 5 and every n ≥ 1, M(x) ≡ k (mod pⁿ) is soluble, and V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅. (b) V_k(ℤ₃) ≠ ∅ if and only if k ≢ ±3 (mod 9), and then M(x) ≡ k (mod 3ⁿ) is soluble for every n; if k ≡ ±3 (mod 9) there is no solution modulo 9. (c) V_k(ℤ₂) ≠ ∅ if and only if k ≢ 3 (mod 4); if k ≡ 3 (mod 4) there is no solution modulo 4. Hence V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for every prime p if and only if k is admissible, equivalently M(x) ≡ k (mod m) is soluble for every m ≥ 1 if and only if k is admissible.
hypotheses: k ∈ ℤ; solubility modulo every power of p is equivalent to V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ by compactness of ℤ_p³ (or directly, since each case below gives an exact p-adic point).
proofSteps: (a) CA.4/markoff-explicit-local-points over ℤ_p (2 and 3 are units for p ≥ 5).

(b) Modulo 3 the only solution of M(x) ≡ 0 is 0 (if all coordinates are units the squares sum to 0 but the product is ±1; if one vanishes, the other two squares sum to 0). So 3 | k forces all x_i ≡ 0 (mod 3) and then M(x) ≡ 0 (mod 9): no solution for k ≡ ±3 (mod 9). Exact 3-adic points otherwise: k ≡ 1 (mod 3): (√k, 0, 0); k ≡ 2 (mod 3): (0, √(k − 1), 1); k ≡ 9 (mod 27): (√k, 0, 0); k ≡ 18 (mod 27): (3y, 3, 0) with y² = k/9 − 1 ≡ 1 (mod 3); 27 | k: (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. The square roots exist in ℤ₃ because the radicands are ≡ 1 (mod 3) (hensels_lemma for T² − c).

(c) Modulo 4, k ≡ 3 is not a value of M (a case check over (ℤ/4ℤ)³). Exact 2-adic points: k even: (x₁, 1, 1) with x₁ a root of T² − T + 2 − k, which exists by Hensel since the derivative 2T − 1 is a unit and the root exists modulo 2; k ≡ 1 (mod 8): (√k, 0, 0); k ≡ 5 (mod 8): (√(k − 4), 0, 2); these square roots exist in ℤ₂ since the radicands are ≡ 1 (mod 8).

The admissibility statement combines (a)–(c); the corrected lifts at p = 2, 3 are those of the extraction's source issues PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E2–E3, which the source's own proof misses (the printed lifts from (3, 0, 0) mod 9 and (1, 0, 0) mod 4 reach only part of the classes).
acceptance: k = 46: admissible (46 ≡ 2 mod 4, 46 ≡ 1 mod 9), so V₄₆(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for every p although V₄₆(ℤ) = ∅.
k = 18 and k = 5 are the classes missed by the printed lifts; (3·1, 3, 0) = (3, 3, 0) has M = 18 and (1, 0, 2) has M = 5.
Checked: M(x) ≡ k is soluble modulo 16, 27, 25 and 49 exactly for the admissible k with −30 ≤ k < 60 (computation).

sources.match: Local solubility modulo every prime power except for k ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k ≡ ±3 (mod 9), proved by explicit points for p ≥ 5, by Hensel lifting of nonsingular points, and by the analysis modulo 9 and modulo 4 for p = 3, 2.
The congruence obstructions define the admissible levels.

nodes.title: The quadratic-reciprocity obstruction on V_{4+d}(ℤ) (Ghosh–Sarnak (8.1)–(8.2))
nodes.statement: Let d be a nonzero integer, k = 4 + d and x ∈ V_k(ℤ). For {i, j, l} = {1, 2, 3} put w = 2x_i − x_jx_l; then w² − 4d = (x_j² − 4)(x_l² − 4). Consequently every odd prime q with q | x_j² − 4 and q ∤ d has d a nonzero square modulo q (legendreSym q d = 1). In the source's form: if n ↦ (4d/n) is a primitive real character modulo 4d and S_d = {n : (4d/n) ∈ {0, 1}}, then x_j² − 4 ∈ S_d (mod 4d) for j = 1, 2, 3; by quadratic reciprocity this is a congruence condition on x_j modulo 4d that local solubility does not impose, so strong approximation for V_k(ℤ) fails modulo 4d.
hypotheses: d ≠ 0 integer, x an integral point; q odd prime not dividing d.
The character form needs (4d/·) to be a primitive Dirichlet character modulo 4d (a Kronecker symbol); the prime-factor form needs nothing.
proofSteps: The identity is (1) of CA.4/markoff-delta-differences with k − 4 = d.
If q | x_j² − 4 then w² ≡ 4d (mod q); as q ∤ 2d, d ≡ (w/2)² is a nonzero square modulo q.

Character form: (4d/·) is multiplicative and (4d/q) = (d/q) = 1 for the odd prime factors q ∤ d of x_j² − 4, while the prime factors dividing 4d give the value 0 or are absorbed; so the character of x_j² − 4 is 0 or 1. Quadratic reciprocity (jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity) rewrites (d/q) through congruences on q, hence on x_j.
acceptance: k = 46 (d = 42): the odd prime factors of x_j² − 4 not dividing 42 are quadratic-residue primes for 42; this is consistent with V₄₆(ℤ) = ∅.
Every point (2, t, t + w) of V_{4+w²} has x₁² − 4 = 0, the degenerate case of the statement.

sources.match: For k = 4 + d the factorisation w² − 4d = (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) forces every prime factor of x_j² − 4 into the multiplicative set where the character (4d/·) takes the values 0 or 1, which by quadratic reciprocity is a congruence condition not implied by local solubility.

nodes.title: Hasse failures k = 4 ± 2ν² (Ghosh–Sarnak, Proposition 8.1 (i)–(ii))
nodes.statement: (i) Let ν ≥ 3 be odd with every prime factor ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8), and k = 4 − 2ν² < 0. (ii) Let ν ≥ 1 have every prime factor ≡ ±1 (mod 8) and ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9), and k = 4 + 2ν² > 4. In both cases k is admissible (so V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for all p) and V_k(ℤ) = ∅: k is a Hasse failure.
hypotheses: (i) ν odd and ≥ 3 (ν = 1 gives k = 2 > 0, outside the case).
(ii) The source lists ν ∈ {0, ±3, ±4} (mod 9); the prime-factor condition gives 3 ∤ ν, so ν ≢ 0, ±3 (mod 9), and admissibility at 3 (ν² ≡ 7 mod 9) forces ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9).
proofSteps: Admissibility: ν odd gives 4 ± 2ν² ≡ 2 or 6 (mod 8), so k ≢ 3 (mod 4); modulo 9, in (i) k ≡ 4, 2, 5 or 8 (no ±3), and in (ii) ν² ≡ 7 (mod 9) gives k ≡ 0. Local solubility then follows from CA.4/markoff-local-solubility.

Some coordinate is odd: 4 ± 2ν² ≡ 2 (mod 4), and three even coordinates give M ≡ 0 (mod 4). Say x₁ is odd, so x₁² − 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8). In case (i) |x₁| ≥ 3 (CA.4/markoff-descent-negative-level), so x₁² − 4 > 0, and as products of primes ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8) are ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8), it has a prime factor q ≡ 5 or 7 (mod 8). In case (ii) x₁² − 4 is positive or equal to −3, and as products of primes ≡ ±1 (mod 8) are ≡ ±1 (mod 8), it has a prime factor q ≡ ±3 (mod 8) (q = 3 when x₁ = ±1).

q ∤ ν by the hypothesis on the prime factors of ν; by CA.4/markoff-reciprocity-obstruction with d = ∓2ν², w² ≡ ∓8ν² (mod q), so −2 (case (i)) or 2 (case (ii)) is a square modulo q, contradicting the supplementary laws (ZMod.exists_sq_eq_neg_two_iff for q ≡ 5, 7 mod 8; ZMod.exists_sq_eq_two_iff for q ≡ ±3 mod 8).
acceptance: (i) ν = 3, 9, 11 give the Hasse failures k = −14, −158, −238; (ii) ν = 23 gives k = 1062, which is admissible, generic and has F⁺₁₀₆₂(ℤ) = ∅ (computation).
ν = 1 in (ii) gives k = 6, which is not admissible (6 ≡ −3 mod 9): the congruence on ν is needed.

sources.match: For k = 4 + 2εν² with ν odd and its prime factors in the stated classes, an odd coordinate x₁ makes x₁² − 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8), whose prime factor in the excluded classes would make ±2 a quadratic residue by (8.4); local solubility comes from Proposition 6.1.

nodes.title: Hasse failures k = 4 + 2ℓ² for primes ℓ ≡ ±4 (mod 9) (Ghosh–Sarnak, Proposition 8.1 (iii))
nodes.statement: Let ℓ ≥ 13 be a prime with ℓ ≡ ±4 (mod 9) and k = 4 + 2ℓ². Then k is admissible and not exceptional, and V_k(ℤ) = ∅. The smallest such k is 342 (ℓ = 13).
hypotheses: ℓ prime, ℓ ≥ 13, ℓ ≡ ±4 (mod 9); no condition on ℓ modulo 8.
proofSteps: Admissible: k ≡ 2 (mod 4) and k ≡ 0 (mod 9).

Not exceptional: at least two coordinates of a point are odd (k ≡ 2 mod 4); a coordinate 0 forces x₂² + x₃² = 4 + 2ℓ² with x₂, x₃ odd, but the left side is ≡ 2 and the right ≡ 6 (mod 8); a coordinate ±1 gives (2x₂ ∓ x₃)² + 3x₃² = 4(3 + 2ℓ²), so 8ℓ² ≡ 2 would be a square modulo 3 (this corrects the misprinted display of the source, PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E7); a coordinate ±2 gives (x₂ ∓ x₃)² = 2ℓ², impossible.

So k is generic and by CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets every point is equivalent to (−u₁, u₂, u₃), u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ); then u₁ ≤ k^{1/3}, u₂ ≤ (k/u₁)^{1/2}, and two of the u_j are odd, so some odd u_j ≤ √(k/3).

u_j² − 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) has a prime factor q ≡ ±3 (mod 8). If q ≠ ℓ, CA.4/markoff-reciprocity-obstruction with d = 2ℓ² makes 2 a square modulo q, a contradiction. If q = ℓ then ℓ | u_j ± 2, so ℓ − 2 ≤ u_j ≤ √((4 + 2ℓ²)/3), which forces ℓ ≤ 11.
acceptance: k = 342, 1062 (ℓ = 23) and 1926 (ℓ = 31) are Hasse failures (computation).
Unlike (i)–(ii), this family uses the fundamental set, and it is not explained by the integral Brauer–Manin obstruction (Loughran–Mitankin, Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu, as reported by the source).

sources.match: For k = 4 + 2ℓ² with ℓ ≥ 13 prime and ℓ ≡ ±4 (mod 9), the fundamental set bounds an odd coordinate by √(k/3), which excludes the prime factor ℓ, and the non-exceptionality of k is checked directly; the smallest such k is 342.
The families (i)–(ii) are accounted for by the integral Brauer–Manin obstruction, while (iii) uses reciprocity together with Markoff descent.

nodes.title: Hasse failures k = 4 + 12ν² (Ghosh–Sarnak, Proposition 8.2)
nodes.statement: Let ν satisfy ν² ≡ 25 (mod 32) and have every prime factor ≡ ±1 (mod 12), and k = 4 + 12ν². Then k is admissible and V_k(ℤ) = ∅. The smallest such ν is 11, with k = 1456 (the source prints ν = 37, k = 16432, which is also an example).
hypotheses: ν odd with ν² ≡ 25 (mod 32) and prime factors in ±1 (mod 12).
proofSteps: Admissible: k ≡ 0 (mod 4) and k ≡ 7 (mod 9).
Write the equation as x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = 4 + 12ν² (one sign changed) with w² − 48ν² = (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4).

All coordinates odd: x_j² − 4 is ≡ 5 (mod 12) or divisible by 3. A prime p ≡ ±5 (mod 12) dividing x_j² − 4 is impossible: p ∤ ν, so w² ≡ 48ν² makes 3 a square modulo p, against reciprocity. So x_j² ≡ 1 (mod 12), x_j ≡ ±1 or ±5 (mod 12), and x_j ≡ ±5 is excluded because one of x_j ∓ 2 is then ≡ ±5 (mod 12) and has such a prime factor. With every x_j ≡ ±1 (mod 12), 9 divides (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) = w² − 48ν², so 3 | w and then 3 | ν, a contradiction.
Mixed parity: one odd and two even coordinates give M ≡ 1 (mod 4) ≠ k; two odd and one even: a Vieta move at the even coordinate gives a point with all coordinates odd, excluded above.

All even: y = x/2 satisfies y₁² + y₂² + y₃² + 2y₁y₂y₃ = 1 + 3ν²; an odd y_j gives 3 a square modulo 8, so all y_j are even; then congruences modulo 16 force y_j ≡ 2 (mod 4) and z = y/2 gives z₁² + z₂² + z₃² + 4z₁z₂z₃ ≡ 7 (mod 8) against 1 + 3(ν² − 1)/4 ≡ 3 (mod 8).
acceptance: ν = 11 (11 ≡ −1 mod 12, 121 ≡ 25 mod 32): k = 1456 is admissible, generic, and F⁺₁₄₅₆(ℤ) = ∅ (computation); this corrects the source's claim that 37 is the smallest ν (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E8).
ν = 37 gives k = 16432, also a Hasse failure (computation).

sources.match: For k = 4 + 12ν² with ν² ≡ 25 (mod 32) and prime factors ≡ ±1 (mod 12), the cases of odd coordinates are excluded by reciprocity for the prime factors of x_j² − 4 via (8.6), mixed parity by a Vieta move, and all-even points by congruences modulo 8 and 16.

nodes.title: Hasse failures k = 4 + 20ν² (Ghosh–Sarnak, Proposition 8.3)
nodes.statement: Let ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9) have every prime factor ≡ ±1 (mod 20), and k = 4 + 20ν². Then k is admissible and V_k(ℤ) = ∅. The smallest such ν is 41, with k = 33624.
hypotheses: ν with prime factors in ±1 (mod 20) and ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9).
proofSteps: Admissible: k ≡ 0 (mod 4) and k ≡ 0 (mod 9).
Identity w² − 80ν² = (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) (CA.4/markoff-delta-differences with d = 20ν²).

All coordinates odd. An odd prime p ≡ ±2 (mod 5) dividing some x_j² − 4 is impossible: p ∤ ν, so 80ν² ≡ w² makes 5 a square modulo p, against quadratic reciprocity. If 5 | x_j, the odd numbers x_j ∓ 2 are ≡ ±2 (mod 5) and so have such a prime factor (the source states this for all x_j; it holds for odd x_j only, PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E9). Hence 5 ∤ x_j and x_j² − 4 ≡ −3 or 5 (mod 20). If x_j² − 4 ≡ −3 (mod 20), then x_j² − 4 ≡ 2 (mod 5) again has an odd prime factor ≡ ±2 (mod 5) (the source misprints the class as 3, PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E10). So x_j² − 4 ≡ 5 (mod 20) for every j, and 25 | w² − 80ν² forces 5 | ν, a contradiction.

Mixed parity: one odd and two even coordinates give M ≡ 1 (mod 4) ≠ k; two odd and one even: a Vieta move at the even coordinate gives an all-odd point. All even: y = x/2 gives y₁² + y₂² + y₃² + 2y₁y₂y₃ = 1 + 5ν² with w₀² − 5ν² = (y₁² − 1)(y₂² − 1); all y_j even contradicts 1 + 5ν² ≡ 2 (mod 4), and an odd y_j gives 8 | y_j² − 1, so 5 would be a square modulo 8.
acceptance: ν = 41: k = 33624 is admissible, generic, and F⁺₃₃₆₂₄(ℤ) = ∅ (computation).
The source's congruence x₁² − 4 ≡ 3 (mod 20) is misprinted for −3 (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E10).

sources.match: For k = 4 + 20ν² the same scheme as Proposition 8.2 with the squares modulo 20 and reciprocity for 5, ending with the equation y₁² + y₂² + y₃² + 2y₁y₂y₃ = 1 + 5ν².

nodes.title: Infinitely many Hasse failures of both signs (Ghosh–Sarnak, Theorem 1.2 (i), qualitative form)
nodes.statement: There are infinitely many negative Hasse failures and infinitely many positive Hasse failures: k = 4 − 2·3^{2m} (m ≥ 1) and k = 4 + 2ℓ² for the infinitely many primes ℓ ≡ 4 (mod 9) are all Hasse failures. In particular the Markoff form does not satisfy the integral Hasse principle.
hypotheses: None beyond the families of CA.4/markoff-hasse-failures-two-nu-squared and CA.4/markoff-hasse-failures-prime-family.
proofSteps: ν = 3^m (m ≥ 1) is odd with all prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 8): CA.4/markoff-hasse-failures-two-nu-squared (i) gives the negative family k = 4 − 2·3^{2m}.
Dirichlet's theorem (Nat.forall_exists_prime_gt_and_eq_mod) gives infinitely many primes ℓ ≡ 4 (mod 9), ℓ ≥ 13; CA.4/markoff-hasse-failures-prime-family gives the positive family.
acceptance: The quantitative lower bound of the source is CA.4/markoff-hasse-failure-count-lower-bound.

sources.match: There are infinitely many Hasse failures, deduced from Proposition 8.1; the qualitative statement needs only the infinitude of the families.

nodes.title: The number of Hasse failures up to K is ≫ √K (log K)^{−1/2} (Ghosh–Sarnak, Theorem 1.2 (i))
nodes.statement: As K → ∞, #{0 < k ≤ K : k is a Hasse failure} ≫ √K (log K)^{−1/2} and #{−K ≤ k < 0 : k is a Hasse failure} ≫ √K (log K)^{−1/2}.
hypotheses: The source's phrase 'at least √K (log K)^{−1/2}' is read as ≫ (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E11).
The analytic input is the lower bound for integers whose prime factors lie in a set of primes of relative density 1/2 (Landau–Wirsing); it is a recorded gap here.
proofSteps: Negative k: k = 4 − 2ν² with ν odd and all prime factors ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8) (CA.4/markoff-hasse-failures-two-nu-squared (i)); the number of such ν ≤ √(K/2) is ≫ √K (log K)^{−1/2} by the Landau–Wirsing count for the set of primes ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8), of relative density 1/2.
Positive k: k = 4 + 2ν² with ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9) and all prime factors ≡ ±1 (mod 8) (case (ii)); the same count restricted to a residue class modulo 9 gives the same order.
Distinct ν give distinct k.
acceptance: Family (i) has 1, 5, 13 and 113 members with |k| ≤ 10², 10³, 10⁴ and 10⁶ (computation), that is about 0.21, 0.42, 0.39 and 0.42 times √K (log K)^{−1/2}; this illustrates the order of growth and proves nothing about it.

sources.locator: §1, Theorem 1.2 (i), p. 5, and §8, the paragraph after Proposition 8.1, p. 24
sources.match: The counts of positive and negative Hasse failures are at least of order K^{1/2}(log K)^{−1/2}, the density of the families of Proposition 8.1.

nodes.title: The first Hasse failures: h_M(46) = 0, h_M(−2) = 1, and −4 (Ghosh–Sarnak, consequences (a)–(b))
nodes.statement: (a) V₄₆(ℤ) = ∅, so 46 is a Hasse failure, and it is the smallest positive one: every admissible k with 0 ≤ k ≤ 45 has V_k(ℤ) ≠ ∅. (b) h_M(−2) = 1, every point of V₋₂(ℤ) being Γ-equivalent to (3, 3, 4); and −4 is the largest negative Hasse failure (−1 and −3 are not admissible and V₋₂(ℤ) ≠ ∅).
hypotheses: Integral points; admissibility as in CA.4/markoff-level-classification.
proofSteps: (a) 46 is generic (CA.4/markoff-level-classification) and F⁺₄₆(ℤ) = ∅ because the polynomial is ≥ 54 on u_j ≥ 3, so CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets (i) gives V₄₆(ℤ) = ∅; 46 is admissible.

For 0 ≤ k ≤ 45: k = 0 (two orbits), 1, 2 (CA.4/markoff-levels-one-to-three), 4 (the Cayley cubic) have points; every admissible 5 ≤ k ≤ 45 is exceptional (a finite check of the three binary equations), hence has points.
(b) F⁻₋₂(ℤ) = {(3, 3, 4)} (a finite search in the box U(−2)), so CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets (ii) gives h_M(−2) = 1; F⁻₋₄(ℤ) = ∅ and −4 is admissible, so V₋₄(ℤ) = ∅.
acceptance: The source's own verification that 46 is not exceptional: 46 is not a sum of two squares, 42 is not a square, and x₂² + x₃² − x₂x₃ = 45 forces 3 | x₂, x₃ and then u₁² + 3u₂² = 20, impossible modulo 5.
The next positive Hasse failures are 56, 86, 124, 126, 142, 161, 198, and the negative ones begin −4, −8, −14, −18, −19 (computation).

sources.match: V₄₆(ℤ) is empty and 46 is the first positive Hasse failure; h_M(−2) = 1 with all solutions equivalent to (3, 3, 4); −4 is the first negative Hasse failure.
The verification that 46 is a Hasse failure through Theorem 1.1 and the non-exceptionality of 46.

nodes.title: Upper bounds for the class numbers at non-exceptional levels (Ghosh–Sarnak, consequence (c))
nodes.statement: (a) For every integer k ≥ 5, |F⁺_k(ℤ)| ≤ 2k^{2/3}; for every k < 0, |F⁻_k(ℤ)| ≤ 2(|k| + 9). Hence h_M(k) ≤ 2|k|^{2/3} for k ≥ 5 not exceptional and h_M(k) ≤ 2(|k| + 9) for k < 0. (b) For every ε > 0, h_M(k) ≪_ε |k|^{1/3 + ε} as |k| → ∞ through levels k ≥ 5 that are not exceptional and through k < 0.
hypotheses: (b) is the source's bound, restricted to non-exceptional levels, which is the range its argument covers (source issue ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E553).
The input of (b), a bound ≪_ε N^ε for the number of unit-classes of solutions of X² − (a² − 4)Y² = 4N uniform in a, is a recorded gap.
proofSteps: (a) For u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ): 3u₁² + u₁³ ≤ k gives u₁ ≤ k^{1/3}, and u₁u₂² ≤ u₁u₂u₃ ≤ k gives u₂ ≤ (k/u₁)^{1/2}; u₃ is the unique positive root of a quadratic. Summing (k/u₁)^{1/2} over u₁ ≤ k^{1/3} gives ≤ 2k^{2/3}. For F⁻_k use the box U(k) of CA.4/markoff-descent-negative-level, with at most two values of u₃ for each (u₁, u₂). The class-number statement is CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets.

(b) Fix u₁ = a ≥ 3 and put N = k − a²; the pairs (u₂, u₃) satisfy (2u₃ + au₂)² − (a² − 4)u₂² = 4N, a norm equation in the order of discriminant a² − 4, on which the unit (a + √(a² − 4))/2 acts. The fundamental-set inequalities a ≤ u₂ ≤ u₃ (and u₃ ≤ au₂/2 for k < 0) cut out a region meeting each unit-orbit in O(1) points.

The number of unit-orbits of solutions is at most the number of solutions b (mod 2N) of b² ≡ a² − 4 (mod 4N), summed over the square divisors of N, which is ≪_ε N^ε by the divisor bound (the recorded gap).
Summing over a ≤ |k|^{1/3} gives ≪_ε |k|^{1/3+ε}.
acceptance: At the exceptional levels k = 4 + w² the points (2, t, t + w) lie in ⌊w/2⌋ + 1 different orbits for w ≤ 20 (computation), so no bound of order |k|^{1/3+ε} is claimed there.

sources.match: h_M(k) ≪ |k|^{1/3+ε}, because for each fixed first coordinate the fundamental sets bound the number of units acting on the indefinite binary quadratic form in the other two variables.

nodes.title: Degree descent for polynomial parametric solutions (Ghosh–Sarnak, Lemma 5.1)
nodes.statement: Let ε = ±1, α_j, β_j ∈ ℤ and M*(x) = Σ_j α_jx_j + β₁x₂x₃ + β₂x₁x₃ + β₃x₁x₂ + x₁² + x₂² + εx₃² − x₁x₂x₃, and k ∈ ℤ. If P₁, P₂, P₃ ∈ ℤ[t] all have positive degree and M*(P₁, P₂, P₃) = k identically, then there are q ∈ ℤ and Q₁, Q₂ ∈ ℤ[t] of positive degree with M*(q, Q₁, Q₂) = k, or M*(Q₁, q, Q₂) = k, or M*(Q₁, Q₂, q) = k identically (one coordinate constant). No identity M*(P₁, P₂, P₃) = k holds with exactly two of the P_j constant and the third of positive degree.
hypotheses: Polynomials over ℤ; 'parametric solution' means a polynomial map t ↦ (P₁(t), P₂(t), P₃(t)) into M* = k.
proofSteps: Degrees d_j = deg P_j ≥ 1: comparing the top degree of M*(P) forces the largest degree to be the sum of the other two (equal degrees, or two equal maxima, would leave the cubic term uncancelled); say d₃ = d₁ + d₂.

The quadratic εx₃² + (β₁x₂ + β₂x₁ + α₃ − x₁x₂)x₃ + (rest) in x₃ has a second root x₄ with x₃ + x₄ = ε(x₁x₂ − α₃ − β₁x₂ − β₂x₁) and x₃x₄ = ε(x₁² + x₂² + β₃x₁x₂ + α₁x₁ + α₂x₂ − k); so P₄ = ε(P₁P₂ − α₃ − β₁P₂ − β₂P₁) − P₃ is a polynomial solution with d₃ + d₄ ≤ 2 max(d₁, d₂), hence d₄ < max(d₁, d₂).
Replacing P₃ by P₄ lowers the maximal degree; repeat (with the move in whichever coordinate has the largest degree) until some coordinate becomes constant.
With two constants q₁, q₂ the identity reads εP₃² + (linear in P₃) + const = k, impossible for deg P₃ ≥ 1 since ε = ±1.
acceptance: For M itself (all α_j, β_j = 0, ε = 1) the curve (t(t + w) − 2, t, t + w) on V_{4+w²} has degrees (2, 1, 1); one descent step, the move in the first coordinate, returns the line (2, t, t + w).
The second-root formula of the source has sign slips that do not affect the degree count (source issue ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E552).

sources.match: For the general Markoff-type polynomial M* with ε = ±1, a polynomial parametric solution with all three coordinates nonconstant can be reduced by Vieta moves, lowering the largest degree, to one with a constant coordinate; parametric solutions with two constant coordinates do not exist.

nodes.title: Polynomial parametric families on V_k and on x₁² + x₂² − x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k
nodes.statement: (1) V_k contains a nonconstant polynomial curve t ↦ (P₁(t), P₂(t), P₃(t)) with P_j ∈ ℤ[t] if and only if k − 4 = w² is a square, in which case (2, t, t + w) is one (a line); in particular there is none when k is generic. (2) The surface W_k : x₁² + x₂² − x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k contains such a curve if and only if k + 4 = w² is a square (family (t + w, t, 2)) or k = 0 (family (Q, 0, ±Q) for any Q ∈ ℤ[t]); moreover, for k = 4^α k′ with k′ odd, W_k has the integral point (0, 2^α(k′ + 1)/2, 2^α(k′ − 1)/2).
hypotheses: Polynomials with integer coefficients; a curve is nonconstant if some coordinate has positive degree.

The further claims of the source about W_k (no local obstructions, infinitely many integral points, infinitely many Hasse failures such as k = 94) are not planned: the source asserts them without proof.
proofSteps: By CA.4/markoff-parametric-degree-descent (and the impossibility of two constant coordinates) a nonconstant curve can be taken of the form with one constant coordinate q and two coordinates Q₁, Q₂ of the same positive degree.

(1) Q₁² + Q₂² − qQ₁Q₂ = k − q²: the leading coefficients q₁, q₂ satisfy q₁² + q₂² − qq₁q₂ = 0 with q₁q₂ ≠ 0, so q² − 4 is a square and q = ±2; then (Q₁ ∓ Q₂)² = k − 4 identically, so k − 4 is a square. Conversely (2, t, t + w) works.

(2) With the constant in the third coordinate the computation is the same with k + 4 in place of k − 4, giving (t + w, t, 2). With the constant q in the first or second coordinate, Q₁² − Q₂² − qQ₁Q₂ = k − q² forces q₁² − q₂² − qq₁q₂ = 0 for the leading coefficients, whose discriminant q² + 4 is a square only for q = 0; then (Q₁ − Q₂)(Q₁ + Q₂) = k with Q₁, Q₂ nonconstant forces k = 0 and Q₁ = ±Q₂.
The point: with x₁ = 0, W_k becomes x₂² − x₃² = k, and (2^α(k′ + 1)/2)² − (2^α(k′ − 1)/2)² = 4^α·k′ = k.

nodes.title: Certified enumeration of Markoff class numbers and Hasse failures
nodes.statement: There are computable functions markoffFundamentalSearch : ℤ → Finset (Fin 3 → ℤ), returning F⁺_k(ℤ) for k ≥ 5 and F⁻_k(ℤ) for k < 0 by a search over the explicit boxes, and markoffExceptionalTest : ℤ → Bool, deciding exceptionality by bounded searches for u² + v² = k, u² + 3v² = 4(k − 1) and u² = k − 4. They are correct: the search returns exactly the fundamental set, and the test decides MarkoffExceptional. Consequently, for k ≥ 5 or k < 0: k is a Hasse failure if and only if k is admissible, markoffExceptionalTest k = false and the search returns ∅; and for k not exceptional, h_M(k) is the cardinality of the search result.
hypotheses: k ≥ 5 or k < 0; the levels 0 ≤ k ≤ 4 are settled by CA.4/markoff-levels-one-to-three, CA.4/markoff-coefficient-one-zero-orbits and CA.4/markoff-cayley-cubic-orbits.
The search is complete only because of the proven box bounds; a terminated search without them proves nothing.
proofSteps: Search for k ≥ 5: u₁ ranges over 3 ≤ u₁ with 3u₁² + u₁³ ≤ k, u₂ over u₁ ≤ u₂ with u₁² + 2u₂² + u₁u₂² ≤ k, and u₃ is tested as the positive root of u₃² + u₁u₂u₃ + u₁² + u₂² − k (an integer square-root test).
Search for k < 0: u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ √(|k| + 9) and u₃ the roots of u₃² − u₁u₂u₃ + u₁² + u₂² − k with u₂ ≤ u₃ ≤ u₁u₂/2, inside the box U(k) of CA.4/markoff-descent-negative-level.

Exceptionality test: the three equations have only finitely many candidate (u, v) (|u|, |v| ≤ 2√|k| + 2), decided by Int.sqrt; correctness is the characterisation of CA.4/markoff-level-classification.
Correctness of the Hasse-failure decision and of h_M(k) = |search| is CA.4/markoff-fundamental-sets.
acceptance: The search returns 6 points at k = 3685, 9 at k = −3691, 11 at k = 9454 and 8 at k = 9500 (the source's Table 5 rows, recomputed); it returns ∅ at k = 46 and k = 1456. At k = 3685 the exceptionality test is true, so the six points give only h⁺, not h_M (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion/E554).

Counting k ∈ [5, 100800] admissible, not exceptional, with empty search gives 7630 = A_HF(100800), the first entry of the source's Table 3; there are 7105 further admissible k ≤ 100800 with empty F⁺ that are exceptional and so are not Hasse failures.

nodes.title: Exceptional Markoff–Hurwitz tuples (Gamburd–Magee–Ronan, Definition 15)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1 and k be integers. A point x ∈ V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊) is fundamental exceptional if, after sorting its coordinates increasingly, either (A) a = 1, x₁ = ⋯ = x_{n−3} = 1 and x_{n−2} = 2, or (B) a = 2 and x₁ = ⋯ = x_{n−2} = 1. In case (A) such an x lies in V iff (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = k − n − 1, and in case (B) iff (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = k − n + 2. The exceptional set E ⊆ V_{n,a,k}(ℤ) is the union of the Γ_{n,a}(ℤ)-orbits of the fundamental exceptional points; the other points are unexceptional. E is Γ_{n,a}(ℤ)-invariant; E ≠ ∅ only if a = 1 and k − n − 1 is a square, or a = 2 and k − n + 2 is a square; and when E ≠ ∅ the number of fundamental exceptional points with largest coordinate ≤ R is cR + O(1) for some c > 0.
hypotheses: E is defined with the group generated by moves, permutations and even sign changes (CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-moves); the source uses Aut(V), which contains it.

This notion differs from Ghosh–Sarnak's exceptional levels (a point with a coordinate of absolute value ≤ 2, CA.4/markoff-level-classification): for n = 3, a = 1 only the coordinate-two lines (2, t, t + w) of the level 4 + w² are Gamburd–Magee–Ronan exceptional.
proofSteps: Membership in case (A): Σx_i² = (n − 3) + 4 + x_{n−1}² + x_n² and a∏x_i = 2x_{n−1}x_n, so the equation is (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = k − n − 1; case (B) is the same computation with n − 2 ones.
Invariance of E is immediate from its definition as a union of orbits.

If (x_{n−1} − x_n)² = w² is fixed, the fundamental exceptional points are (1, …, 1, 2, m, m + w) (resp. (1, …, 1, m, m + w)) for m ≥ 2 (resp. m ≥ 1): one for each value of the largest coordinate, which gives the linear count.
acceptance: n = 3, a = 1, k = 8: (2, 2, 4) and (2, 3, 5) are fundamental exceptional ((x₂ − x₃)² = 4 = k − 4).
n = 3, a = 1, k = 14: E = ∅ (10 is not a square), although (1, 3, 4) ∈ V₁₄(ℤ) has a coordinate 1.
n = 4, a = 2, k = 2: (1, 1, t, t) is fundamental exceptional for every t ≥ 1.

nodes.title: From V(ℤ) to V(ℤ₊): sign changes and the bounded error (Gamburd–Magee–Ronan, §2.1)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1, k ∈ ℤ and V = V_{n,a,k}. (a) The set X₀ of points of V(ℤ) ∖ E with a zero coordinate is empty if k < 0 and finite if k ≥ 0 (every coordinate satisfies x_i² ≤ k). (b) The group N of even sign changes acts freely on X = V(ℤ) ∖ (E ∪ X₀), and each N-orbit in X contains either exactly one point with all coordinates positive or exactly one point with x₁ < 0 < x₂, …, x_n; the orbits of the second kind are finite in number (none if k ≤ 0). (c) Consequently, for every R ≥ 0, |(V(ℤ) ∖ E) ∩ B(R)| = 2^{n−1}·|(V(ℤ₊) ∖ E) ∩ B(R)| + O_{n,a,k}(1), with B(R) the ℓ^∞ ball of radius R, and the error term bounded independently of R by |X₀| + 2^{n−1}·(number of orbits of the second kind).
hypotheses: n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1, k ∈ ℤ; E is the exceptional set of CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-exceptional; the ℓ^∞ ball is N-invariant.
proofSteps: (a) A zero coordinate kills the product, so Σx_i² = k.

(b) A point with no zero coordinate is fixed by no nontrivial sign change, so N (of order 2^{n−1}) acts freely; even sign changes preserve the parity of the number of negative coordinates, and within a parity class they act transitively on sign patterns, so each orbit contains the all-positive pattern or the pattern with only x₁ negative, exactly once.
The second kind: x̃ = (−x₁, x₂, …, x_n) has positive coordinates and Σx̃_i² + a∏x̃_i = k, which has no solution for k ≤ 0 and finitely many otherwise (each x̃_i² ≤ k).
(c) E and X₀ are N-invariant; count X by orbits (2^{n−1} points each, all with the same ℓ^∞ norm) and add X₀.
acceptance: n = 3, a = 3, k = 0: X₀ = {0}, there is no orbit of the second kind, and |V(ℤ) ∩ B(R)| = 4·|M ∩ B(R)| + 1 (the four sign patterns with product +1 of CA.4/markoff-tree).
n = 3, a = 1, k = −2: X₀ = ∅ and there are no orbits of the second kind; the positive point (3, 3, 4) accounts for exactly the four integral points (3, 3, 4), (−3, −3, 4), (−3, 3, −4), (3, −3, −4).

nodes.title: Behaviour of the moves outside a compact set (Gamburd–Magee–Ronan, Proposition 16)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1 and k ∈ ℤ. There is R₀ = R₀(n, a, k) such that for every R ≥ R₀, with K₀ = {x : ‖x‖_∞ ≤ R}, every unexceptional x ∈ V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊) ∖ K₀ satisfies: (1) if x_j is a largest coordinate, every coordinate of m_j(x) is < x_j; (2) the largest coordinate of x is attained exactly once; (3) if x_j is not the largest coordinate, then m_j(x)_j is strictly larger than every other coordinate of m_j(x); (4) if x_j is not the largest coordinate, m_j(x) has at least as many distinct coordinates as x; (5) every move m_j maps x into V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊). Part (3) holds only outside K₀ (the source's remark that it holds on all of V(ℤ₊) is false, PAPER-GAMBURD-MAGEE-RONAN-19/E3).
hypotheses: Unexceptional positive tuples; K₀ may be enlarged at will.
proofSteps: Growth: if x_{n−1} < (x_n/(2a))^{1/(n−1)} for a sorted x, then a∏_{i<n}x_i < x_n/2 and x_n² ≤ a∏x_i + k gives x_n² < 2k; so outside a large ball x_{n−1} ≥ (x_n/(2a))^{1/(n−1)} and x_{n−1}² > |k|.

(1) (Cassels' argument) With f(T) = T² − a x₁⋯x_{n−1}T + x₁² + ⋯ + x_{n−1}² − k, whose roots are x_n and m_n(x)_n, failure of (1) gives f(x_{n−1}) ≥ 0, hence a x₁⋯x_{n−2} + k/x_{n−1}² ≤ n, so a x₁⋯x_{n−2} ≤ n: finitely many choices of x₁, …, x_{n−2}. Then either (x_n + x_{n−1})(x_n − x_{n−1}) ≤ x₁² + ⋯ + x_{n−2}² − k (finitely many x), or x_n = x_{n−1} is a root of (2 − a x₁⋯x_{n−2})T² + x₁² + ⋯ + x_{n−2}² − k (finitely many x) unless 2 − ax₁⋯x_{n−2} = 0 and x₁² + ⋯ + x_{n−2}² = k, which are exactly the fundamental exceptional families.
(2) If the largest entry were repeated, the move at one of its positions would not decrease it, against (1).
(3) m_j(x)_j − x_n = x_n(a∏_{i≠j,n}x_i − 1) − x_j > 0 unless a = 1 and x₁ = ⋯ = x_{n−2} = 1; in that remaining case x_{n−1}² + x_n² − x_{n−1}x_n = k − n + 2 has finitely many solutions, added to K₀.
(4) follows from (3); (5): outside a large ball, a x₁⋯x_{n−1} − x_n > 0, since otherwise x₁² + ⋯ + x_{n−1}² ≤ k contradicts x_{n−1}² > |k|.
acceptance: n = 3, a = 1, k = 14: (1, 3, 4) violates (3) (m₂ gives the coordinate 1·4 − 3 = 1), so (3) fails on V(ℤ₊) itself; (1, 3, 4) lies in the compact set.
For n = a = 3, k = 0 one may take K₀ = {(1, 1, 1)} up to permutation: every other Markoff triple has a unique largest entry and the move there decreases it (CA.4/markoff-descent-inequality).

nodes.title: Infinite descent for Markoff–Hurwitz tuples (Gamburd–Magee–Ronan, Corollary 17)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 3, a ≥ 1, k ∈ ℤ and K₀ as in CA.4/markoff-hurwitz-moves-outside-compact. Every unexceptional x ∈ V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊) is carried into K₀ by a finite sequence of moves, each at the (unique) largest coordinate and each strictly decreasing the largest coordinate; the sequence is determined by x. Hence the unexceptional positive tuples lie in the union of the orbits, under the moves, of the finitely many points of V_{n,a,k}(ℤ₊) ∩ K₀. For n = a = 3, k = 0 this is Markoff's theorem: every Markoff triple reduces to (1, 1, 1) (CA.4/markoff-root-generation).
hypotheses: Unexceptional positive tuples; the descent is algorithmic because at each step the largest coordinate is unique and the move there is forced.
proofSteps: Outside K₀ the move at the largest coordinate keeps the point in V(ℤ₊) (property (5)) and decreases the maximum (property (1)); unexceptionality is preserved because E is invariant.
The maximum is a positive integer, so after finitely many steps the point lies in K₀.
Reversing the steps exhibits x in the orbit of a point of K₀; K₀ ∩ V(ℤ₊) is finite.
acceptance: n = a = 3, k = 0: K₀ ∩ V(ℤ₊) can be taken to be the permutations of (1, 1, 1), (1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 5) or just {(1, 1, 1)}, recovering CA.4/markoff-root-generation.
n = a = 4, k = 0 (Hurwitz): (3, 1, 1, 1) reduces to (1, 1, 1, 1) by the move at the coordinate 3.

nodes.title: The negative-Pell radicands 𝒟⁻ and the family 𝒟 (Koymans–Pagano)
nodes.statement: 𝒟 is the set of squarefree integers d > 0 all of whose prime factors are ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 4) (that is, p = 2 or p ≡ 1 mod 4), and 𝒟⁻ is the set of squarefree integers d > 0 for which x² − dy² = −1 has a solution x, y ∈ ℤ. For real X, 𝒟(X) = {d ∈ 𝒟 : d < X} and 𝒟⁻(X) = {d ∈ 𝒟⁻ : d < X}, finite sets. One has 1 ∈ 𝒟⁻ ((x, y) = (0, 1)), 𝒟⁻ ⊆ 𝒟 (proved in CA.4/negative-pell-rational-solubility), and the inclusion is strict (34 ∈ 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟⁻).
hypotheses: d > 0 squarefree; d = 1 is included in both sets.

For d > 1 the integral solubility is the solubility of the negative Pell equation of CA.4/negative-pell-classification; the comparison with units of norm −1 in quadratic orders and with class groups belongs to CA.5.
proofSteps: Define 𝒟 and 𝒟⁻ as subsets of ℕ cut out by Squarefree and the stated conditions; the truncations are Finset.filter on Finset.range ⌈X⌉ (they are finite since d < X).
A negative d has no solution since x² + |d|y² ≥ 0 > −1, so imposing d > 0 loses nothing.
34 ∉ 𝒟⁻: x² − 34y² = −1 has no integral solution (Dummit's Problem 5(d); also checked through the continued fraction of √34, whose period has even length), while 34 = 2·17 ∈ 𝒟.

nodes.title: Rational solubility of the negative Pell equation
nodes.statement: Let d > 0 be squarefree. The following are equivalent: (i) x² − dy² = −1 has a solution x, y ∈ ℚ; (ii) d is a sum of two squares of integers; (iii) every prime factor of d is 2 or ≡ 1 (mod 4), i.e. d ∈ 𝒟. Consequently 𝒟⁻ ⊆ 𝒟. A congruence or rational criterion is not an integral one: d = 34 has the rational solution (5/3, 1/3) but no integral solution.
hypotheses: d > 0 squarefree (for d not squarefree (ii) and (iii) differ, e.g. d = 9).
proofSteps: (i) ⇒ (ii): clearing denominators, X² + Z² = dY² with Y ≠ 0; so dY² is a sum of two squares, hence (Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff) every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) divides dY² to an even power, hence does not divide the squarefree d, and d is a sum of two squares.
(ii) ⇔ (iii): Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff for squarefree d.
(ii) ⇒ (i): if d = u² + v² with v ≠ 0 then (x, y) = (u/v, 1/v) solves x² − dy² = −1; if v = 0 then d = u² is squarefree, so d = 1 and (0, 1) works.
This is the elementary form of the Hasse–Minkowski argument the source cites (−1 is a norm from ℚ(√d) everywhere locally).
acceptance: d = 34 = 3² + 5²: (5/3, 1/3) is a rational solution.
d = 3, 6, 21 have no rational solution (3 | d with 3 ≡ 3 mod 4).

sources.match: Solubility of the negative Pell equation over ℚ is necessary for solubility over ℤ, and by Hasse–Minkowski it holds exactly when every prime factor of d is ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4).
A prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) of D rules out solutions, through x² ≡ −1 modulo that prime.

nodes.title: Dirichlet's theorem: x² − py² = −1 is soluble for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4)
nodes.statement: For every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) the equation x² − py² = −1 has a solution in integers, i.e. p ∈ 𝒟⁻. In particular 𝒟⁻ is infinite.
hypotheses: p prime with p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
proofSteps: Let (x₁, y₁) be the fundamental solution of x² − py² = 1 (Pell.IsFundamental.exists_of_not_isSquare; p is not a square).
x₁ is odd: if x₁ were even then y₁ would be odd and x₁² − py₁² ≡ −p ≡ −1 ≢ 1 (mod 4). Hence y₁ is even and gcd(x₁ − 1, x₁ + 1) = 2.
From (x₁ − 1)(x₁ + 1) = p y₁²: either x₁ − 1 = 2ps², x₁ + 1 = 2t², or x₁ − 1 = 2s², x₁ + 1 = 2pt², with s, t > 0 and y₁ = 2st.
In the first case t² − ps² = 1 with 0 < t < x₁, contradicting minimality; so the second case holds and s² − pt² = −1.

nodes.title: Coefficientwise identities of infinite products specialise along ring homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let φ : A →+* B be a ring homomorphism, (f_i) a family in A⟦X⟧ and g ∈ A⟦X⟧ such that for every m the coefficient of X^m of the finite products ∏_{i∈s} f_i is eventually (in the filter of finite sets s) equal to the coefficient of X^m of g. Then the same holds for (PowerSeries.map φ (f_i)) and PowerSeries.map φ g, and HasProd (map φ ∘ f) (map φ g) holds in B⟦X⟧ with PowerSeries.WithPiTopology for every topology on B. The same holds for sums.
hypotheses: A, B commutative rings; no topology on A is needed for the hypothesis.
proofSteps: coeff_m(map φ (∏_{i∈s} f_i)) = φ(coeff_m ∏_{i∈s} f_i) (PowerSeries.coeff_map and map_prod), so eventual equality transfers.
In PowerSeries.WithPiTopology convergence is coefficientwise (tendsto_iff_coeff_tendsto); an eventually constant sequence converges in any topology.
acceptance: Applied to Mathlib's pentagonal number theorem (coeff_prod_one_sub_X_pow_eventually_eq) it gives the identity in B⟦X⟧ for every ring B, as Mathlib already states for each R.

sources.match: Identities of partition generating functions are identities of formal power series, proved coefficientwise; the coefficient of a given degree of an infinite product is determined by finitely many factors.

nodes.title: Jacobi's triple product identity in formal power series
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring with a Hausdorff topology (any topology for the multipliability and the coefficient form), and give R⟦x⟧ the pi topology (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology). (a) For a ∈ Rˣ the family n ↦ (1 − x^{2n})(1 + a x^{2n−1})(1 + a⁻¹x^{2n−1}) (n ≥ 1) is multipliable, n ↦ aⁿx^{n²} (n ∈ ℤ) is summable, and ∏_{n≥1}(1 − x^{2n})(1 + a x^{2n−1})(1 + a⁻¹x^{2n−1}) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} aⁿx^{n²}. (b) For s ∈ Rˣ, in R⟦t⟧: ∏_{i≥1}(1 − tⁱ)(1 + s tⁱ)(1 + s⁻¹t^{i−1}) = Σ_{k∈ℤ} s^k t^{k(k+1)/2}. Equivalently, the coefficients of the finite products are eventually equal to those of the sums. The universal cases are R = ℤ[a, a⁻¹] (Mathlib's LaurentPolynomial ℤ, a = T 1), of which every other case is the image under a ring homomorphism.
hypotheses: R commutative and a, s units of R. The coefficient form needs no topology; the HasProd form holds for every topology on R, and writing the bilateral sum as a tsum assumes R Hausdorff (as Mathlib's tprod form of the pentagonal theorem does).

The analytic identity for complex parameters, J(z; q) := (z; q)_∞(q/z; q)_∞(q; q)_∞ = Σ_{k∈ℤ}(−1)^k q^{k(k−1)/2} z^k for 0 < |q| < 1 and z ≠ 0, is owned by GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic (Layer 4, §4.3, the triple product behind its Gauss identity); this node is its formal counterpart.
proofSteps: Coefficients: the coefficient of x^m of the finite products in (a) stabilises once 2n − 1 > m, and is a Laurent polynomial c_m(a) ∈ ℤ[a, a⁻¹]; likewise in (b) once i > m.

Complex case: (a) is J(−zx; x²) and (b) is J(−s⁻¹; t), because (−zx; x²)_∞ = ∏_{n≥1}(1 + z x^{2n−1}), (x²/(−zx); x²)_∞ = ∏(1 + z⁻¹x^{2n−1}), (x²; x²)_∞ = ∏(1 − x^{2n}) and Σ_k(−1)^k x^{k(k−1)}(−zx)^k = Σ_k z^k x^{k²}; similarly for (b) after k ↦ −k. For z ∈ ℂ^× and |x| < 1 the product converges absolutely and its expansion Σ_m c_m(z)x^m converges (majorant with |z|, |z|⁻¹, |x|), so the analytic identity and uniqueness of power-series coefficients (HasFPowerSeriesAt.eq_formalMultilinearSeries) give, for every z ∈ ℂ^× and m > 0, c_m(z) = zⁿ + z⁻ⁿ if m = n² with n > 0 and c_m(z) = 0 if m is not a square, and the analogous coefficients in (b).
A Laurent polynomial over ℤ vanishing on ℂ^× is zero (multiply by a power of T and use Polynomial.eq_zero_of_infinite_isRoot), so the coefficient identities hold in ℤ[a, a⁻¹].

Specialise along the ring homomorphism ℤ[a, a⁻¹] → R sending a to the given unit, by CA.4/power-series-product-specialisation; multipliability and summability are Mathlib's order criteria in the pi topology.
A purely formal alternative avoiding analysis is Pak's bijective proof of (b) (attach a Sylvester triangle to a Young diagram and split it along a diagonal).
acceptance: Coefficients of x⁰, …, x⁴ in (a): 1, a + a⁻¹, 0, 0, a² + a⁻² (computation of the finite product with n ≤ 3).

Consistency with Mathlib's pentagonal number theorem (PowerSeries.WithPiTopology.hasProd_one_sub_X_pow): in (b) the substitution t = x³, s = −x⁻¹ is legitimate coefficientwise (s^k t^{k(k+1)/2} becomes ±x^{k(3k+1)/2}, a nonnegative exponent) and turns the product into ∏(1 − x^{3i})(1 − x^{3i−1})(1 − x^{3i−2}) = ∏(1 − xⁿ) and the sum into Σ(−1)^k x^{k(3k+1)/2}.

sources.match: The triple product ∏(1 − x^{2n+2})(1 + x^{2n+1}z)(1 + x^{2n+1}z⁻¹) = Σ x^{n²}zⁿ for z ≠ 0, |x| < 1, derived from Euler's two identities; valid for |x| < |z| and then by analytic continuation.

The triple product identity in the forms Σ zⁿq^{n²} = ∏(1 − q^{2k})(1 + zq^{2k−1})(1 + z⁻¹q^{2k−1}) and Σ s^k t^{k(k+1)/2}∏(1 − tⁱ)⁻¹ = ∏(1 + stⁱ)(1 + s⁻¹t^{j}) (j ≥ 0), with a direct bijective proof by splitting a Young diagram along a diagonal.

nodes.title: Jacobi's identity ∏(1 − xⁿ)³ = Σ (−1)ⁿ(2n + 1)x^{n(n+1)/2}
nodes.statement: In R⟦x⟧ for every commutative ring R (any topology, pi topology on R⟦x⟧): ∏_{n≥1}(1 − xⁿ)³ = Σ_{n≥0} (−1)ⁿ(2n + 1) x^{n(n+1)/2}, the product multipliable and the sum summable; equivalently (1/2)Σ_{n∈ℤ}(−1)ⁿ(2n + 1)x^{n(n+1)/2} over ℤ, where the terms n and −n − 1 coincide.
hypotheses: R commutative; the identity has integer coefficients and is the image of the case R = ℤ.
proofSteps: Start from form (b) of CA.4/jacobi-triple-product in ℤ[s, s⁻¹]⟦t⟧: Σ_k s^k t^{k(k+1)/2} = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − tⁱ)(1 + stⁱ)(1 + s⁻¹t^{i−1}).

Put s = −w: the factor i = 1 of the last product is 1 − w⁻¹, and pairing k with −k − 1 on the left gives (1 − w⁻¹)·∏_{i≥1}(1 − tⁱ)(1 − wtⁱ)(1 − w⁻¹tⁱ) = Σ_{k≥0}(−1)^k w^{−k−1}(w^{2k+1} − 1)t^{k(k+1)/2}.
1 − w⁻¹ is a non-zero-divisor in ℤ[w, w⁻¹]⟦t⟧, so ∏(1 − tⁱ)(1 − wtⁱ)(1 − w⁻¹tⁱ) = Σ_k (−1)^k w^{−k}(1 + w + ⋯ + w^{2k}) t^{k(k+1)/2}.
Specialise w ↦ 1 (CA.4/power-series-product-specialisation): 1 + w + ⋯ + w^{2k} ↦ 2k + 1.
acceptance: Coefficients up to x⁶: 1, −3, 0, 5, 0, 0, −7.
This is the identity (i) of Hirschhorn's proof of Jacobi's four-square theorem.

nodes.title: The theta-product specialisations of the triple product
nodes.statement: In R⟦x⟧ for every commutative ring R (any topology, pi topology): (ii) ∏_{n≥1}(1 + x^{2n−1})²(1 − x^{2n}) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} x^{n²}; (iii) 2·∏_{n≥1}(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n}) = Σ_{r∈ℤ} x^{r²+r}, equivalently ∏_{n≥1}(1 + x^{2n})²(1 − x^{2n}) = Σ_{r≥0} x^{r(r+1)} (the form valid over every ring, since the terms r and −r − 1 coincide); (iv) (x; x)_∞ = (−x; x)_∞ · Σ_{n∈ℤ}(−1)ⁿ x^{n²}, i.e. ∏(1 − xⁿ)/(1 + xⁿ) = Σ(−1)ⁿx^{n²}, where (−x; x)_∞ = ∏(1 + xⁿ) is a unit; and Euler's identity (−x; x)_∞ · ∏_{n≥1}(1 − x^{2n−1}) = 1.
